findings.lesson_text: Sherriff served as a captain in the trenches and was seriously wounded at Passchendaele in 1917.
findings.issue: The Key Fact box states Sherriff 'served as a captain in the trenches.' Sherriff was commissioned as a Second Lieutenant and was still a Second Lieutenant (or at most a Lieutenant) when he was wounded at Passchendaele on 2 August 1917. He only held the temporary rank of Captain from January 1919, after the war ended, as an assistant area gas officer. Calling him a 'captain' is anachronistic and incorrect for his front-line service.
findings.canonical_truth: R.C. Sherriff held the rank of Second Lieutenant when he served in the trenches and was wounded at Passchendaele in 1917. He served with the 9th Battalion East Surrey Regiment. He reached the rank of temporary Captain only after the war, in 1919.

findings.lesson_text: His line 'It's the only way to forget' is one of the play's most important. It tells us that Stanhope is self-aware — he knows he is damaged — but has no other way to cope.
findings.issue: The lesson treats 'It's the only way to forget' as a key Act 1 line from Stanhope, implying it is delivered early in the play as self-aware reflection on his drinking. This phrase does not appear verbatim in the play. The actual closest line — 'To forget, you little fool — to forget! D'you understand? To Forget! You think there's no limit to what a man can bear?' — is from Act 3 Scene 2, when Stanhope rounds on Raleigh after Osborne's death. The Act 1 Stanhope drinking quote is 'She doesn't know that if I went up those steps into the front line — without being doped with whiskey — I'd go mad with fright.' Students memorising 'It's the only way to forget' as an Act 1 quote will misplace it by two acts in the exam.
findings.canonical_truth: Stanhope's key Act 1 drinking quote is 'She doesn't know that if I went up those steps into the front line — without being doped with whiskey — I'd go mad with fright' (Act 1, p.31). The 'forget' language appears in Act 3 Scene 2: 'To forget, you little fool — to forget! D'you understand? To Forget!' The paraphrase 'It's the only way to forget' does not appear to be a verbatim line from the play.

findings.lesson_text: Raleigh's description of Stanhope as 'the one man I could talk to as a friend' establishes the schoolboy bond...
findings.issue: The lesson attributes 'the one man I could talk to as a friend' to Raleigh (about Stanhope). The actual quote 'the one man I could trust — my best friend — the one man I could talk to as man to man — who understood everything' is Stanhope's line about Osborne, spoken in Act 3 Scene 2 after Osborne's death. These are two different contexts that have been conflated. Raleigh does describe Stanhope as a school hero, but in his letter and in Act 1 he uses different phrasing ('Dennis is the finest officer in the battalion, and the men simply love him'). Attributing Stanhope's grief-stricken tribute to Osborne to Raleigh describing Stanhope will mislead students in their exam analysis.
findings.canonical_truth: The line 'the one man I could talk to as man to man — who understood everything' is spoken by Stanhope about Osborne in Act 3 Scene 2, expressing his devastation at Osborne's death. Raleigh's praise for Stanhope in his letter reads 'Dennis is the finest officer in the battalion, and the men simply love him.' These are distinct quotes by different characters in different acts.

findings.lesson_text: His line 'You think there's no limit to what a man can bear?' This line reveals the immense pressure Stanhope is under.
findings.issue: The lesson presents 'You think there's no limit to what a man can bear?' in the Act 1 section as part of Stanhope's reaction to Raleigh's arrival. According to multiple sources, this line is part of Stanhope's speech in Act 3 Scene 2 — 'To forget, you little fool — to forget! D'you understand? To Forget! You think there's no limit to what a man can bear?' — which is addressed to Raleigh after Osborne's death, during the confrontation about the celebration dinner. It does not appear in Act 1.
findings.canonical_truth: The full passage 'To forget, you little fool — to forget! D'you understand? To Forget! You think there's no limit to what a man can bear?' is Stanhope's outburst at Raleigh in Act 3 Scene 2, not Act 1. It is delivered after Osborne's death when Raleigh refuses to eat at the celebration dinner.

findings.lesson_text: Stanhope tells Hibbert: 'If you went — Loss of Raleigh's map will be — irreplaceable.' He threatens to shoot Hibbert if he leaves, but then admits his own terror.
findings.issue: This Key Fact box attributes a quote to Stanhope that is corrupted and nonsensical: 'If you went — Loss of Raleigh's map will be — irreplaceable.' The words 'Raleigh's map' and 'irreplaceable' do not appear in the Stanhope–Hibbert confrontation. The real Stanhope speech to Hibbert in Act 2 Scene 2 concerns letting down fellow soldiers: 'If you went — and left Osborne and Trotter and Raleigh and all those men up there to do your work — could you ever look a man straight in the face again — in all your life!' The phrase 'Raleigh's map' appears nowhere in the play's key confrontations. This appears to be a garbled or AI-generated corruption of the real speech, and the fabricated text could mislead students into citing a quote that does not exist.
findings.canonical_truth: Stanhope's actual speech to Hibbert in Act 2 Scene 2: 'If you went — and left Osborne and Trotter and Raleigh and all those men up there to do your work — could you ever look a man straight in the face again — in all your life!... Don't you think it worth standing in with men like that?' No reference to 'Raleigh's map' or 'irreplaceable' exists in any authoritative source for this scene.

findings.lesson_text: The censorship of Raleigh's letter...One of Act 2's most revealing scenes occurs when Stanhope insists on reading Raleigh's letter home before it is sent.
findings.issue: The lesson assigns the letter-censorship scene to Act 2 generally without specifying a scene. This is accurate (it is Act 2 Scene 1) and no direct error. However, the lesson states 'When Osborne reads the letter aloud, it contains nothing but admiration' — this description is correct. No error here but worth noting the lesson conflates Act 2 into one undifferentiated block, which is not wrong but slightly imprecise for students who need to cite specific scenes.
findings.canonical_truth: The letter-censorship scene is Act 2 Scene 1. Stanhope has Osborne read it aloud. The letter praises Stanhope: 'Dennis is the finest officer in the battalion, and the men simply love him.' The Hibbert confrontation is Act 2 Scene 2.

findings.lesson_text: The Colonel selects Osborne and Raleigh to lead the raiding party...He offers Osborne a box of cigars as a reward, a detail that highlights the grotesque disparity between the commanders behind the lines and the men who face death.
findings.issue: The lesson says the Colonel offers Osborne 'a box of cigars as a reward' as an incentive before the raid. According to multiple sources, it is champagne, cigars, and a fresh chicken that arrive as a celebration after the raid's completion (Act 3 Scene 2), not a personal gift from the Colonel to Osborne before it. The Colonel promises a Military Cross recommendation if the raid succeeds, not cigars. Presenting cigars as a pre-raid incentive offered directly to Osborne misrepresents both the timing and the source of the gift.
findings.canonical_truth: The Colonel promises to recommend Osborne and Raleigh for the Military Cross if the raid succeeds. The champagne, cigars, and fresh chicken arrive after the raid (Act 3 Scene 2) as a celebration provided by the higher command, not as a personal pre-raid gift from the Colonel to Osborne. Osborne does not receive the cigars — he is dead by Act 3.

findings.lesson_text: Stanhope is a brilliant and dedicated commander — the Colonel calls him 'the best company commander in the battalion'
findings.issue: The lesson states 'the Colonel calls him the best company commander in the battalion.' This quote is Osborne's, not the Colonel's. Osborne says 'He's a long way the best company commander we've got' (Act 1) in response to Hardy's mockery of Stanhope's drinking. The Colonel does not use this phrase. Attributing it to the Colonel misidentifies the speaker and changes the dramatic significance: Osborne's defence of Stanhope is a mark of loyalty; if the Colonel said it, it would merely be a professional assessment. Exam students citing this as a Colonel quote would be wrong.
findings.canonical_truth: Osborne says 'He's a long way the best company commander we've got' in Act 1 when defending Stanhope to Hardy. The Colonel does not use this phrasing. The same error appears in the lesson 7 Key Fact box ('Stanhope is called the best company commander in the battalion') without attribution — that form is acceptable but this lesson explicitly misattributes to the Colonel.

findings.lesson_text: Osborne is the oldest officer in the company, a former schoolmaster and rugby player, and the emotional heart of the group.
findings.issue: Describing Osborne as simply 'a rugby player' understates a significant character detail. Osborne played rugby for England — he is a former international rugby player. This is repeatedly cited across authoritative sources as part of Osborne's characterisation: a man of genuine achievement and quiet distinction who mentions it only modestly. A student writing about Osborne's background and class values would be missing an important detail.
findings.canonical_truth: Osborne is a former schoolmaster who played rugby for England (an England rugby international). This detail emphasises his pre-war stature and contrasts with his humble, self-effacing manner in the dugout. Sources confirm: 'Osborne is humble and, despite playing rugby for England, does not boast about his achievements.'

findings.lesson_text: Raleigh's description of Stanhope as 'the one man I could talk to as a friend' establishes the schoolboy bond that Stanhope fears the war has destroyed.
findings.issue: Same error as L02: the lesson attributes 'the one man I could talk to as a friend' to Raleigh (about Stanhope). The actual quote — 'the one man I could trust — my best friend — the one man I could talk to as man to man — who understood everything' — is Stanhope's tribute to Osborne, spoken in Act 3 Scene 2 after Osborne is killed. Raleigh's praise for Stanhope in his letter is 'Dennis is the finest officer in the battalion, and the men simply love him.' The conflation of these two quotes (one by Raleigh about Stanhope, one by Stanhope about Osborne) appears in both L02 and L05, and will cause students to misattribute a key Act 3 speech.
findings.canonical_truth: Stanhope says 'the one man I could trust — my best friend — the one man I could talk to as man to man' about Osborne in Act 3 Scene 2. Raleigh's letter about Stanhope says 'Dennis is the finest officer in the battalion, and the men simply love him.' These are two separate quotes by different characters in different acts.

findings.lesson_text: Stanhope's heroism is inseparable from his damage: 'It's the only way to forget.'
findings.issue: The Key Fact box presents 'It's the only way to forget' in quotation marks as a Stanhope line about heroism and endurance. This phrasing does not appear verbatim in the play. The actual line Stanhope says about drinking is either 'She doesn't know that if I went up those steps into the front line — without being doped with whiskey — I'd go mad with fright' (Act 1) or 'To forget, you little fool — to forget! D'you understand? To Forget!' (Act 3 Scene 2). The phrase 'It's the only way to forget' as a self-contained quotation does not match either. Students memorising this as an exam quotation risk writing a line that cannot be verified in the play text.
findings.canonical_truth: The verbatim Stanhope drinking quote from Act 1 is 'She doesn't know that if I went up those steps into the front line — without being doped with whiskey — I'd go mad with fright.' The Act 3 Scene 2 outburst is 'To forget, you little fool — to forget! D'you understand? To Forget! You think there's no limit to what a man can bear?' The phrase 'It's the only way to forget' appears to be a paraphrase, not a direct quotation.

findings.lesson_text: Raleigh describes Stanhope as 'the one man I could talk to as a friend,' but the Stanhope he finds is a damaged stranger who sees Raleigh as a threat.
findings.issue: Third instance of the same misattribution (also in L02 and L05): 'the one man I could talk to as a friend' is attributed to Raleigh describing Stanhope. The actual quote 'the one man I could talk to as man to man' is Stanhope describing Osborne in Act 3 Scene 2. The repeated appearance of this error across three lessons indicates it was introduced by the content generation pipeline and carried through all subsequent lessons.
findings.canonical_truth: This line is Stanhope's tribute to the dead Osborne, not Raleigh's praise for Stanhope. The error appears identically in L02, L05, and L07, suggesting systematic pipeline contamination.
